How to enter a competition

Competition calendars are published by clubs, national federations and FITASC, and you can also find events on ClayArena. Once you have chosen an event in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting, read its programme first. It usually tells you:

  1. the dates, the place and the discipline;
  2. the number of targets and the format;
  3. the schedule, the entry deadline and the entry fee;
  4. the categories and the prizes;
  5. the organiser’s contacts and any local rules.

An entry is your registration for the competition. It is often made online in advance and confirmed at the desk on the day. The entry fee is paid with the entry or at registration. Ask early whether the fee is refunded if you cannot come.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Keep the amount of the fee in mind. Some referee decisions can be appealed in writing to the jury (the panel in charge of the competition). In Sporting™ you then leave a deposit of 40% of the entry fee; you get it back if the jury agrees with you. How appeals work: Results, protests and appeals.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 9 · What can go to the jury and the 40% deposit

For official competitions you usually need to be a member of a club or of the national federation. Some federations also issue a sports licence, which is not a gun permit. Shooters for European and World Championships are usually entered by their national federation. These rules differ between countries, so check them early with your federation or the organiser.

Gun laws differ from country to country. You must own your gun and cartridges legally at home and take them legally to where you shoot. If you live in the EU and take your own gun to another EU country, you usually need a European Firearms Pass. Each country’s own rules still apply. Details: Travelling with a gun inside the EU.

Tip: The pass is issued only to residents of EU countries and of the Schengen states that apply the EU firearms rules (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein). If you live elsewhere, read Outside the EU: national permits, or ask the organiser whether you can hire a gun at the ground.

This concerns only guns fitted with a release trigger. It fires when the finger lets go, not when it pulls. If the law of the host country bans such triggers, the programme of an international competition must say so.

After entries close, the organiser publishes the shooting times and the squad lists. A squad is a small group of up to six shooters who shoot each round together; the list tells you which squad you are in and when it starts. Keeping to the schedule is your own responsibility, including any delays or changes during the event.

Compak® Sporting

Compak® Sporting can be shot in line: shooters enter station 1 one by one and move along the line to station 5. In this format a shooter who misses the first day is taken off the start list from the second day. To shoot after all, that shooter must appeal to the jury.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 10 · Absent on day one

Tip: Before your first event, write down the date, your squad’s start time, the address of the ground and the organiser’s phone number. Keep the confirmation you received and any gun documents with your kit.

Key points

  • Read the programme first: dates, targets, schedule, fee, categories, contacts.
  • Entries are often made online and confirmed at the desk on the day.
  • Official events usually need club or federation membership; for European and World Championships your federation enters you.
  • Taking your own gun to another EU country usually needs a European Firearms Pass; only residents of the EU and of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein can get it.
  • Keeping to the schedule is your own responsibility.

Did you know?

Where release triggers are allowed, a gun with one carries a fluorescent sticker with a large “R” on the outside of the stock, so that everyone on the stand knows.

For parents
  • For a junior, ask the organiser in advance whether a parent’s written consent or a federation licence is needed, and who may supervise the child at the ground.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What should you read first once you have chosen a competition?

    1. The results of last year’s event
    2. The programme of the competition
    3. The weather forecast for the day
    Answer

    The programme of the competition

    The programme gives the dates, targets, schedule, fee, categories and contacts.

  2. Who is responsible for knowing when your squad shoots?

    1. The referee of the first stand
    2. The organiser, who will phone you
    3. You yourself, as the shooter
    Answer

    You yourself, as the shooter

    The schedule is published in advance, and following it, including changes during the event, is the shooter’s responsibility.

    Chapter 8 · Shooting schedule: the shooter's responsibility

  3. When do you usually need a European Firearms Pass?

    1. When an EU resident takes their own gun to another EU country
    2. Whenever you enter any competition, even in your own country
    3. Only when you hire a gun from a ground in another country
    Answer

    When an EU resident takes their own gun to another EU country

    The pass is for residents of the EU and of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein who travel with their own gun to another of these countries. People who live elsewhere are not issued one.
